content: 1. The lead of the After Action Review (AAR) should send an advanced email communication to introduce the scope, objectives, and processes of the review. This email should also be used to schedule or confirm interviews with participants. 2. The analytical phase of an AAR is the most substantial component, where participants collaboratively identify and agree on challenges and best practices observed during the response. They also develop measures to enhance future capacity. This analysis should adhere to a structured approach, including objective observation, gap analysis, and identification of areas for improvement, guided by pre-selected trigger questions. 3. Facilitation during working group or debrief formats should promote active participation and interaction, focusing on specific areas or sessions. These include identifying existing capacities prior to the event, such as plans, policies, resources, coordination mechanisms, preparedness activities (e.g., immunization), and others. 4. A comprehensive timeline of key milestones should be created to establish a shared understanding of the response's chronology. This timeline should include critical dates such as the start of the outbreak, detection, notification, verification, laboratory confirmation, intervention, public communication, and declaration of the outbreak's end. These milestones help assess the timeliness and adequacy of actions taken. 5. Participants should evaluate the speed of outbreak recognition and response using specific time intervals, such as the time to detection, laboratory confirmation, public communication, and intervention. For disease-specific AARs, the timeline should be interpreted alongside the epidemic curve to assess the impact of interventions on outbreak control. 6. During the session on strengths, challenges, and new capacities, participants should identify enabling factors for best practices, articulate challenges faced, and conduct root cause analysis to address limiting factors. Clear actions should be outlined to embed best practices, address challenges, and strengthen preparedness for future responses. 7. Root cause analysis is a method to identify factors directly contributing to success or failure in a specific issue. It focuses on long-term interventions rather than quick fixes. The five whys technique is commonly used to progressively uncover causative factors and identify the root cause. This method is particularly effective in group discussions during an AAR. 8. Facilitators should ensure that discussions during the AAR are informed by relevant documentation, including the latest publications on the disease or event under review. Highlights of new capacities developed during the response should also be presented for each response pillar. 9. Participants may review the performance of International Health Regulations (IHR, 2005) core capacities during the response, using qualitative ratings such as performed without challenges, performed with some challenges, performed with major challenges, or unable to be performed. These evaluations help assess the extent to which selected capacities were utilized. 10. Consensus-building among participants involves summarizing best practices, challenges, new capacities, and evaluated AAR indicators. This can be achieved through plenary or group discussions to validate results and foster ownership, ensuring corrective actions are implemented. 11. Before closing the AAR, a final working group session should integrate any additional comments or feedback from the debriefing session. For key informant interview formats, draft findings should be shared with all involved for feedback and validation. 12. An evaluation of the AAR workshop and methodology should be conducted before closing to identify areas for improvement. Toolkits provide an evaluation form template for this purpose. 13. The AAR team debriefing should reflect on the planning, preparation, and conduct of the AAR. This informal discussion, led by the AAR lead or main facilitator, aims to identify lessons and opportunities for future projects. It should occur within one week of completing the AAR. 14. Senior management should be briefed on the outcomes of the AAR, including best practices, challenges, and agreed follow-up actions. This briefing seeks to gain support for mobilizing resources and ensures institutional learning and continuous improvement. 15. The AAR can serve as an opportunity for advocacy, resource mobilization, and strategic partnerships. Debriefings with senior government officials, media, technical and financial partners, and other stakeholders can help build collaborations and secure commitments for long-term capacity building. 16. The final AAR report should integrate notes from note-takers and follow a structured template, including an executive summary, background, scope, methods, findings, key activities, next steps, and conclusions. The report should include an action plan with assigned responsibilities, timelines, and costs for implementation. 17. The action plan should prioritize activities based on urgency and resource requirements, categorizing them as short-, medium-, or long-term. Immediate actions with minimal resource needs (quick wins) should be highlighted, alongside longer-term activities requiring integration into broader planning processes. 18. The AAR lead must ensure accountability by assigning activities to specific individuals or authorities, sequencing them appropriately, and monitoring their implementation. Activities should be presented in a clear and actionable format.
